newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil population reaches 157 million - IBGE.
newsitem.headline: Brazil population reaches 157 million - IBGE.

text.p: Brazil's population increased by 11 million between 1991 and 1996 to reach 157 million, but the growth rate was well below previous periods, according to a population census published on Tuesday.
The 1996 census by the National Statistics Institute (IBGE) showed there are 2.2 million more women in the country than men. For every 100 women in Brazil there are 97.26 men.
The number of households headed by women also increased in the five-year period to 20.8 percent from 18.1 percent.

On the whole, Brazil's population grew an average of 1.38 percent a year, well below growth rates in previous decades, with the North and Centre-East of the country experiencing the fastest population growth, the IBGE said.

Although 57 percent of Brazilians live in the Southeast and South of the country, the North, which covers the vast Amazon, saw its population grow 2.44 percent between 1991 and 1996 and the Centre-East, where the capital Brasilia is situated, expanded 2.22 percent, the IBGE said.

Brazil's urban population continued to expand to 78.36 percent of Brazilians in 1996 from 75.59 percent in 1991, mainly as a result of natural growth and rural migration, the IBGE said. The North, Northeast and Centre-East were most strongly affected.
On the whole, Brazil's population is growing older and more educated, the IBGE said. However, the figures on education vary significantly according to region.

The average age of Brazilians has risen to 23.2 years in 1996 as opposed to 21.7 years in 1991, and the number of people with only one year or no education at all has fallen to 10.11 percent among children aged 10 to 14 from as much as 40.99 percent among people aged 60 or older.
The number of children still in school at age 15 to 17 has also increased to 66.8 percent in 1996 from 55.3 percent in 1991.
In the North and Northeast, however, only 11 percent of 15- to 19-year-olds have completed between nine and 11 years of schooling, while in the South and Southeast this figure reaches 25 percent.

The 1996 population census by the National Statistics Institute (IBGE) is the first to complement the IBGE's regular 10-yearly census which is carried out at the beginning of every decade. The IBGE plans to continue having this less extensive type of census at mid-decade.
